title: Mindful Productivity Podcast
author: Sarah Steckler
description: Mindful Productivity is intention and awareness of your current mental state, energy capacity, and external demands that help you better manage how you take action in the present moment to get things done sustainably.

episodes.title: Skills Over Trends: The Mindset Shift for Sustainable Goals & Projects
episodes.summary: Sarah makes the case for building core competencies instead of chasing trends, with an emphasis on experimentation, action over perfectionism, and creating value that doesn't depend on any one platform.

episodes.title: The Big AI Conversation: Why I'm Not Convinced by the Hype
episodes.summary: A long conversation about AI marketing versus reality, what language models can actually do, and why a human voice is important for a small business.

episodes.title: I Finally Deleted Social Media: Here's What Happened to My Business (and My Brain)
episodes.summary: Sarah explains why she deleted every personal and business social media account, how she untangled her business from the platforms, and how marketing through long-form content and SEO is working instead.

episodes.title: The Paper is the Process: My 3-Step Analog System for Idea Capturing
episodes.summary: Why pen-and-paper planning brings clarity and focus, especially for neurodivergent thinkers, and how a simple analog system reduces decision fatigue and boosts memory.

episodes.title: Low Lift Projects for Low Energy Days
episodes.summary: How to stay productive in a business during low-energy stretches: spotting your energy patterns, preparing ahead for slow days, and treating low-energy time as a creative window rather than a failure.

episodes.title: Why Paper Planners Matter More Than Ever in an AI-Filled World
episodes.summary: A look at how analog planning supports deeper thinking and well-being, and how to combine paper planning with digital convenience without the overwhelm.

articles.question: Can you run a business without social media?
articles.metaDescription: Sarah Steckler of the Mindful Productivity Podcast deleted every social account. What happened to her sales, her focus, and her marketing.
articles.intro: Yes, you can run a business without social media, and for some people it works better. Sarah Steckler, host of the Mindful Productivity Podcast, deleted every personal and business account she had and explains in this episode what happened next. Her short version: her marketing shifted to long-form content and search, most of her students were already finding her that way, and her focus came back.

sections.heading: Screen time at 8 to 10 hours a day was the breaking point
sections.body:
Sarah doesn't frame the decision as a strategy first. It started as a health problem. She noticed her brain felt depleted, her energy was low, and her creative capacity was shrinking. Her phone had become what she calls a swirling vortex, and her screen time was hitting 8 to 10 hours a day.

She's honest that willpower wasn't enough. She'd tried limits and breaks before. The habit kept winning, which is why she eventually decided that the only move that would actually stick was deleting the accounts entirely rather than trying to use them less.

That matters for anyone considering the same thing. If you're relying on discipline to keep a platform in its place, and it keeps failing, the episode makes the case that the problem isn't your discipline.

sections.heading: Untangling a business from the platforms takes real steps
sections.body:
Deleting a personal Instagram is one thing. Deleting business accounts that other tools depend on is another. Sarah walks through the practical untangling she had to do before she could hit delete.

She disconnected Facebook logins from apps like Canva, so losing the account wouldn't lock her out of her design tools. She requested her data from the platforms so she'd have a copy of years of posts and messages. And she manually archived her Instagram highlights, since some of that content was still useful for her business.

If you're planning to do the same, that checklist is a good starting point: find every tool that uses a social login, export your data, and save anything you'd actually miss. Then delete.

sections.heading: Search was already doing the heavy lifting
sections.body:
The question everyone asks is whether the business survived. Sarah's answer is that when she looked at the numbers, 85 percent of her students were already finding her through search. Social media wasn't the front door she assumed it was.

So her marketing now leans on what was already working: long-form content and SEO. The podcast itself, her website, and her newsletter carry the weight. She also mails a physical monthly newspaper called The Mindful Moment to her audience, which is about as far from an algorithm as you can get.

The host explains that this shift felt better than ever, not just tolerable. She's flying solo without social media in the business and isn't looking to go back.

sections.heading: What came back: a lighter chest, the library, and birds
sections.body:
The last part of the episode is about what filled the space. Sarah describes a heaviness in her chest that disappeared once she stopped performing her life for an audience. That's a mental health shift, and she treats it as one of the biggest results of the whole experiment.

Her days look different now. She spends time at the library. She watches more birds. She reads more books. She describes being truly present in the moment, which for someone who built a podcast around mindful productivity is the whole point.

None of this required a new tool or a fancier system. It required removing one thing that was quietly eating her time and attention. For a lot of small business owners, the honest math might look the same.

keyTakeaways: Sarah's screen time hit 8 to 10 hours a day and willpower alone couldn't fix it, so she deleted the accounts.
Before deleting, disconnect social logins from tools like Canva, request your data, and archive anything you need.
85 percent of her students already found her through search, so losing social media barely touched her marketing.
Her marketing now runs on long-form content, SEO, a newsletter, and a physical monthly mailer.
The biggest payoff was mental: less heaviness, more presence, and more creative capacity.

faq.q: How do you market a business without social media?
faq.a: Sarah focuses on long-form content and SEO, plus her podcast, newsletter, and a physical monthly mailer. Search was already bringing in most of her students before she deleted anything.

faq.q: What should I do before deleting business social accounts?
faq.a: Disconnect any social logins from other apps, request a copy of your data from each platform, and manually save content like Instagram highlights that you still want.

faq.q: Did deleting social media hurt her business?
faq.a: Based on the episode, no. She says it feels better than ever, and the majority of her customers were already coming from search rather than social.

articles.sourceNote: Based on the Mindful Productivity Podcast episode "I Finally Deleted Social Media: Here's What Happened to My Business (and My Brain)," released March 28, 2026, hosted by Sarah Steckler.
